title: Testing clay porosity and choosing a sealer
subtitle: How to assess whether a dried air-dry clay piece is porous and which sealer to use
excerpt: Air-dry clay pieces must be sealed before use or display, but different pieces have different levels of porosity depending on brand and wall thickness. This technique covers a simple water-drop test to assess porosity and guides the choice between PVA, acrylic varnish, resin coat, and wax sealers.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles and standard clay sealing practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fully air-dried and free of moisture; required before sealing to prevent trapped moisture causing the sealer to blister or crack
The degree to which a clay body allows water to pass through or absorb into it; high porosity means the piece needs sealing before any contact with water

content.text: depending on the clay body formulation and how it was dried. A porous piece that gets wet will absorb moisture and soften, which can cause surface crumbling or deformation. Testing first tells you how urgently sealing is needed and which sealer will give a good result.
Place a single drop of water on an inconspicuous area of the bone-dry piece. Observe for 30 seconds.

If the drop beads up and sits on the surface, the clay body has low porosity and may need only one or two light sealer coats. If the drop soaks in immediately and the clay darkens, the piece is highly porous and needs a thorough sealing sequence.

PVA diluted 50/50 with water: the standard first choice for display-only pieces. Two or three coats give good moisture resistance and act as a base for paint or gold leaf. Dries slightly flexible, which helps if the piece is thick and still moves very slightly as humidity changes.

Acrylic varnish (matte, satin, or gloss): harder surface than PVA, suitable for pieces that will be handled regularly. Brush on in thin coats. Must be applied over a sealed base as it can soak into high-porosity clay and dry patchy.
Two-part epoxy resin: the most water-resistant option; suitable for vessels that may hold dry items. Not suitable for pieces that contact food or hold water, and fumes require ventilation.

Always apply the first sealer coat thinly on a bone-dry piece and allow to dry completely before the second coat. Thick first coats trap air in a porous clay and cause bubbling. Apply two PVA coats as a base before adding any decorative finish such as acrylic paint or gold leaf.

items.problem: Sealer coat bubbles on the clay surface
items.cause: The clay was not fully bone-dry when sealing, so moisture escaped through the sealer as it dried
items.fix: Wait until the piece is completely bone-dry (pale, uniform colour, no cool feel when held to the cheek). Let the piece dry further, then apply a fresh thin sealer coat

items.problem: Acrylic varnish looks patchy and uneven
items.cause: The first varnish coat was applied directly to unsealed porous clay and soaked in unevenly
items.fix: Always seal with two coats of diluted PVA first. The PVA evens out porosity so subsequent varnish coats go on uniformly
